docs.title: Mohar documentation
docs.text:
Mohar is an open-source trust layer for AI agents. It records every agent action as a signed, hash-chained receipt, lets an agent earn permission one capability at a time from outcomes that were actually checked, takes that permission away the moment a gated action fails, and sends only the actions an agent hasn't earned to a person.

Status

Mohar is early. The receipt log and the mohar CLI are released (0.1). The trust engine, the escalation flow and the host adapters are designed and in progress; the roadmap and its milestones say exactly what exists.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Install and first log: install mohar, record decisions, verify the chain, and see what happens when someone edits or truncates it.
  • CLI reference: every command and flag.
  • Design: capabilities, trust levels and the rules that move them, verification, escalation, receipts, privacy and the threat model.
  • Receipts and checkpoints: the formats, with test vectors and an independent checker.
  • Integrations: how Mohar plugs into Claude Code, Codex, CAO, ADK, MCP and A2A, and how strong each seam is.
  • Compliance: how Mohar maps onto HIPAA, GDPR, SOC 2, ISO 27001 and 42001 and the EU AI Act, control by control.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: These docs are versioned. The selector at the top switches between latest (the newest release), each release, and dev (the main branch). Docs for a release never change after it ships.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Releases are cut by the maintainer when the merged work since the last tag adds up to something a user would notice. Never on a fixed schedule.

  1. Open an issue for the release, then a branch.
  2. Move the entries under ## [Unreleased] in CHANGELOG.md into a new ## [x.y.z] - YYYY-MM-DD section and update the compare links at the bottom.
  3. Bump version in crates/mohar-core/Cargo.toml and crates/mohar-cli/Cargo.toml, and the mohar-core version that mohar-cli depends on. Run cargo check so Cargo.lock follows.
  4. Open the pull request. The Release workflow runs dist plan on it, so a broken release configuration fails before anything is tagged.
  5. After it merges and main is green, tag the merge commit and push the tag:
git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "vX.Y.Z"   # use -s instead once a signing key is set up
git push origin vX.Y.Z

Only admins can create v* tags. 6. The Release workflow (generated by cargo-dist; regenerate with dist generate after editing dist-workspace.toml, never by hand) builds mohar for Linux and macOS on x86_64 and arm64 and for Windows on x86_64, writes shell and PowerShell installers and checksums, attests build provenance, and publishes the GitHub Release with the changelog section as its notes. 7. Check one artefact's provenance:

gh attestation verify mohar-cli-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.xz -R harshitwandhare/mohar

Upgrading cargo-dist: change cargo-dist-version, run dist generate, and re-check .github/zizmor.yml, whose accepted findings point at line numbers in the generated file.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: Dates are targets. Each phase is a GitHub milestone, and every task in it is an issue with "Done when" criteria: see milestones. Everything built is held to the engineering bar. Each phase ships as small pull requests against issues that say what "done" means.

docs.title: Phase 0: foundation (Oct to Nov 2026)
docs.text:
• Repository standards: CI, security scanning, contribution rules for humans and agents.
  • Landing page and docs site.
  • Design notes for the receipt format, the trust model and the escalation flow.

docs.title: Phase 1: receipts (Nov to Dec 2026)
docs.text:
• Rust core: Ed25519 keys, a hash-chained append-only log, signed receipts for each action.
  • mohar CLI: init, log, verify.
  • Test vectors other implementations can run.

docs.title: Phase 2: first host, Claude Code (Dec 2026 to Jan 2027)
docs.text:
• Hook adapter that records every tool call and its result.
  • Outcome verifiers: test runs and git diffs.

docs.title: Phase 3: trust per capability (Jan to Mar 2027)
docs.text:
• Capability taxonomy, per-capability scores, hard veto gates, and demotion in proportion to what a failure could have cost, with remediation plans and lessons the agent is given next time.
  • Promotion only from verified outcomes, over a minimum window.

docs.title: Phase 4: escalation (Mar to May 2027)
docs.text:
• Route out-of-bounds actions to the right person.
  • A small per-person model of past yes/no decisions, allowed only to skip prompts on low-risk, reversible actions inside limits that person set.

docs.title: Phase 5: benchmark (May to Aug 2027)
docs.text:
• Public, reproducible benchmark: false promotion rate, time to demotion, prompts avoided at a fixed incident rate, poisoning reaching durable memory.
  • Write-up of methods and results.

docs.title: Phase 6: integrations (Aug 2027 onward)
docs.text:
• MCP proxy, CAO, Google ADK, Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit, Paperclip.
  • One mohar-hook binary with profiles for Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Antigravity CLI and other hosts, each set to fail closed, and a CI check that refuses agent commits without verifying receipts.
  • Agent contributors on open-source repos: start untrusted, earn rights through merged, verified work.

docs.title: Phase 7: enterprise (alongside Phases 4 to 6)
docs.text:
• Auditor evidence pack: an offline-verifiable export with control mappings and configurable retention.
  • Approver protections: two-person approval, independent reinstatement after serious failures, escalation budgets and batching.
  • Cost per verified outcome by agent, person and team, from the hosts' own cost telemetry.

docs.title: Not planned
docs.text: • Another identity provider, policy language, orchestrator or memory store. Good ones exist; Mohar connects to them.

docs.title: How Mohar is meant to sustain itself
docs.text: Mohar is a non-commercial open-source project today. Nothing is sold, there are no paid plans, and no money is accepted. This page sets out how a sustainable model could work later, so that the open-source decisions made now don't close it off.

docs.title: What stays free, always
docs.text:
Everything a single developer or a single team needs to run Mohar on their own machines:

  • the daemon, the CLI and the receipt log;
  • every adapter and plugin (Claude Code, Codex, CAO, ADK, MCP and the rest);
  • the trust engine, verifiers and escalation;
  • the benchmark and its data.

All of it is Apache-2.0, including the right to run it commercially. The name "Mohar" is the only thing not covered by the license.

docs.title: Where value could be charged for, later
docs.text:
The model that works for infrastructure like this, used by companies such as Grafana, PostHog, Sentry and Supabase, is a free core with paid help for organisations operating it at scale. For Mohar that would mean:

Offering Who needs it Why it isn't in the free core A hosted service for teams: shared receipt storage, cross-machine trust, an approvals inbox Teams of 10 or more running many agents It's operating a service, not software Org tree sync from the identity provider and HR system (Okta, Entra, Google Workspace) Companies with more than a few hundred people Connectors to enterprise systems need ongoing maintenance Compliance exports mapped to the EU AI Act, SOC 2 and ISO 42001 Regulated deployers Each framework needs dated, maintained mappings Support, security response commitments and long-term support releases Enterprises A service-level promise, not code

docs.title: Partnerships before revenue
docs.text:
Integrations come before any of that, because a trust layer is only useful where agents already run:

  1. Upstream first. Land the seams Mohar needs (for example pre-action veto events in CAO) as ordinary contributions to those projects, useful even without Mohar.
  2. Plugins in each project's own catalogue. Claude Code plugins, ADK plugins, Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit plugins.
  3. Standards work. Test vectors and reference code for the IETF delegation drafts and A2A, rather than a competing format.

docs.title: What would trigger a company
docs.text: A company would be formed only when all three hold: people outside the project depend on Mohar in production, at least a few organisations ask for something in the paid column above, and the maintainer is in a position to run a company properly. Until then the project takes no sponsorships, bounties or grants.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to Mohar are written here. The format follows Keep a Changelog, and versions follow Semantic Versioning. Before 1.0, minor versions may change the receipt format; each such change is called out.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• The trust engine (mohar_core::trust): trust per agent per capability from verified outcomes weighted by a 30-day half-life, promotion one level at a time on the 95% Wilson lower bound with minimum counts, 7 days at a level and 14 quiet days after a serious failure, never above the capability's ceiling. Failures are classed S0 to S4: near misses and minor slips change no level, three minor slips in 14 days count as one meaningful failure, a meaningful failure drops one level, a serious one drops the capability and those sharing its scope to Ask first, and an integrity failure suspends the agent until a person reinstates it. Demotions start a remediation that blocks promotion until five consecutive verified passes. An irreversible high-risk action goes to a person at every level. The daemon decides from this ledger and rebuilds it from the signed log on start (#48).
  • A capability policy (.mohar/policy.json): named capabilities with a risk tier, a reversibility flag and a ceiling, and ordered rules mapping a host tool and a path or command glob onto them. The first match wins; anything unmatched or outside the project root is unclassified and treated as the highest risk. Invalid files are refused with the reason. The daemon now classifies every action itself, so a decide request no longer carries a capability (#47).
  • mohar daemon: a local service on a loopback address that answers POST /v1/decide and POST /v1/outcome, signs every answer into the log, refuses malformed or oversized requests, answers 503 past a limit of requests in flight, and rebuilds decisions still waiting for an outcome after a crash (#43).
  • mohar hook claude-code and a Claude Code plugin in integrations/claude-code: every tool call asks the daemon first and is allowed, sent to the person, or denied; the hook denies when the daemon is unreachable and only talks to loopback addresses. Until the trust engine ships, reads run and everything else asks (#44).
  • Receipts can carry an optional verification object recording the outcome of an earlier decision. Receipts without it are byte-for-byte unchanged.
  • Fuzz targets for receipt parsing and verification, checkpoint parsing, the log file readers, and a mutation check that any edited log which still parses fails verification. They run for 60 seconds on pull requests that touch crates/ or fuzz/, and for 15 minutes each week (#58).
  • A log can only be opened for writing by one process at a time; a second writer gets a clear error instead of interleaving receipts. Reading and verifying never need the lock (#40).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Verifying a log of a million receipts now takes about 8 seconds instead of about 15.5 on a 6-core laptop. Receipts are parsed, canonicalised, hashed and signature-checked on a worker pool that lives for the whole walk, and canonical JSON is written by a fixed template that tests compare against serde_jcs on arbitrary receipts. Every check and every error is unchanged (#59).
  • New mark: मो in Modi script on a gold octagonal seal, used for the favicon, the site header, the docs site, the README and link previews. The site gains a web manifest and a social preview image.
  • The home page is rebuilt as a board of filled tiles with no photographs: a terminal fragment and two figures, the simulator with a departure-board receipt log, the four steps as one bar sized by how long each takes, receipt fields, trust levels, integrations and a closing action row.
  • The hero stamp is a modelled object: a turned rosewood handle with carved vine bands and an engraved brass die, built by tools/stamp/build_stamp.py in Blender and loaded as a 1.5 MB Draco-compressed glTF.
  • Verifying and opening a log now read receipts.jsonl line by line and check checkpoints as the receipts go past, so memory use no longer grows with the size of the log. A new ChainVerifier checks one receipt at a time, store::verify_file and store::verify_log use it, and signatures are checked on all available cores. mohar verify and mohar log stream too; log --last N keeps only N receipts. verify and verify_checkpoints work as before (#59).
  • The website scales its type and spacing down to phones, has one header with a menu on every page, and uses one button system. A test fails if any page scrolls sideways at 320px (#78).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • The simulator's trust meters showed full at every level in production, because the CSP blocked the inline width they were drawn with. The test server now sends the production headers, so tests run under the real CSP.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • Signatures and public keys must be lowercase hex. Uppercase spellings were accepted, so the last receipt in a log could be rewritten without failing verification. Found by the new fuzz targets (#58).
The first release: a signed, hash-chained receipt log and the mohar command line tool.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Receipts: each decision about an agent action is a JSON record signed with Ed25519 over its RFC 8785 canonical form, and linked to the previous receipt by SHA-256. verify reports the first receipt that was edited, removed or reordered, and why (#15).
  • A log on disk: a directory with the signing key (owner-only on Unix), the public key and receipts.jsonl. Every receipt is synced before append returns, and a log that doesn't verify, or whose last line was cut short, is refused rather than extended (#23).
  • Signed checkpoints, written every 1,000 receipts and on request, so receipts removed from the end of a log are detected (#25).
  • The mohar CLI: init, append, log, checkpoint and verify. verify needs only the public key, so a log can be checked by someone who can't sign (#23, #25).
  • Test vectors for the receipt and checkpoint formats, with an independent Python checker that shares no code with the Rust implementation (#27).
  • Documentation: design (trust levels, verifiers, escalation, receipts, privacy, threat model), integrations, compliance with US and EU rules, and how the project sustains itself.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • CI on Linux, macOS and Windows; CodeQL, OpenSSF Scorecard, gitleaks, cargo-deny, zizmor and an 85% line-coverage floor on every pull request; branch protection on main; release tags limited to admins; release artefacts carry GitHub build attestations.

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
mohar [--dir <path>] <command>

--dir is the log directory, .mohar by default. It applies to every command.

Exit status: 0 on success, 1 when verify finds a break, 2 on any other error (the message goes to standard error).

docs.title: mohar init
docs.text: Creates a new log in --dir: key.ed25519 (the signing seed, owner-only on Unix), public.key, an empty receipts.jsonl and checkpoints.jsonl. Refuses to touch a directory that already holds a log.

docs.title: mohar append
docs.text:
Signs and appends one receipt, then prints its sequence number. The receipt is synced to disk before the command returns.

Flag Meaning --agent Agent identifier --capability Capability the action falls under, such as fs.edit.docs --tool The host tool that would run it --target The path, branch or host it acts on --args-sha256 SHA-256 of the exact arguments --result allow, escalate or deny --level The agent's trust level on this capability (default 0) --by What decided it: gate, score, human or predicted (default human)

Opening the log verifies the whole chain and its checkpoints first; a log that doesn't verify is refused rather than extended. Only one process may write to a log at a time.

docs.title: mohar checkpoint
docs.text: Signs a checkpoint over the log as it stands (how many receipts, and the hash of the last one). A checkpoint is also written automatically every 1,000 receipts.

docs.title: mohar log [--last N]
docs.text: Prints receipts, oldest first, one per line. Doesn't need the signing key or the writer lock.

docs.title: mohar verify [--public-key <file>]
docs.text: Checks every receipt and every checkpoint against the public key (public.key in the log directory by default). Prints ok: ... or the first break with its index and reason. Doesn't need the signing key, so anyone can verify a log they were given.

docs.title: mohar daemon [--addr <host:port>] [--max-inflight <n>]
docs.text:
Serves decisions and outcomes to agent hosts on this machine, from the log in --dir, which it holds open for writing while it runs. It listens on 127.0.0.1:7878 by default and refuses any address that isn't loopback. It prints listening on <address> once bound, and how many earlier decisions are still waiting for an outcome.

Two endpoints, JSON in and out:

POST /v1/decide   {agent, tool, target, args_sha256, call_id?}  ->  {result, level, receipt_seq}
POST /v1/outcome  {receipt_seq | call_id, verifier, result, evidence_sha256}  ->  {receipt_seq}

result is allow, escalate or deny. verifier is tests, diff, replay, human or host; host is the host's own report that a tool ran and never counts toward trust. Unknown fields, bad hashes and oversized bodies are refused with a 4xx and recorded nowhere. Past --max-inflight requests at once (default 64) the daemon answers 503 rather than queueing.

The daemon decides which capability an action falls under from its policy (below); a request can't name one. The trust engine then answers from the agent's verified record on that capability (design, section 4): actions with risk none run; at Ask first everything else goes to a person; at Supervised low-risk reversible actions run; at Trusted actions run inside the capability's gates; an irreversible high-risk action always goes to a person; a suspended agent is denied. Every answer is a signed receipt.

Trust is rebuilt from the log each time the daemon starts, by replaying every verified outcome; it is stored nowhere else. An outcome counts only from a real verifier (tests, diff, replay, human) with a pass or fail result; a host report or an unknown result never does. A failure's severity comes from its capability: low-risk reversible failures are minor, medium-risk ones meaningful, and high-risk or irreversible ones serious. Until remediation plans can name what a pass must exercise (#87), every verified pass counts toward ending remediation.

docs.title: The policy file
docs.text:
The daemon reads <dir>/policy.json when it starts and refuses to start if the file is invalid. Without one it uses a built-in policy rooted at its working directory. A policy names capabilities and an ordered list of rules; the first rule that matches an action's tool and target wins:

{
  "version": 1,
  "root": "..",
  "capabilities": {
    "fs.edit.docs": { "risk": "low",  "reversible": true,  "ceiling": 2 },
    "db.migrate":   { "risk": "high", "reversible": false, "ceiling": 1 }
  },
  "rules": [
    { "tools": ["Edit", "Write"], "paths": ["docs/**"], "capability": "fs.edit.docs" },
    { "tools": ["Bash"], "commands": ["*migrate*"], "capability": "db.migrate" }
  ]
}
  • risk is none, low, medium or high; ceiling is the highest level an agent may reach on the capability, 0 to 2, and a high-risk irreversible capability can't go above 1.
  • A rule gives either paths (globs over the target relative to root, where * and ? stay within a directory and ** crosses directories) or commands (globs over the whole command line, where * matches anything), never both. tools limits it to those host tools.
  • root defaults to the directory that holds the log directory. .. in a target is resolved first, so a path can't climb out of the root.
  • An action that matches no rule, or names a path outside the root, is unclassified: high risk, irreversible, ceiling 0.
  • Unknown fields, unknown capability names in rules and the reserved name unclassified are refused.

The built-in policy (mohar_core::policy::BUILTIN) is a fuller example: reads, docs, tests, code and config edits, read-only shell commands, pushes to a branch and to the default branch.

After a crash, decisions without an outcome are rebuilt from the log on the next start and can still be given one by receipt_seq; call_ids live only for the life of the process.

docs.title: mohar hook claude-code [--daemon <url>]
docs.text: The command Claude Code runs for PreToolUse and PostToolUse. It reads the hook payload on stdin, asks the daemon, and prints Claude Code's permissionDecision: allow, ask (for escalate) or deny. It denies when the daemon can't be reached, answers with an error, or the payload can't be read, and it only ever talks to a loopback address. PostToolUse is recorded as a host outcome matched by tool_use_id. Subagents are identified as agent:claude-code/<agent_type>, the main agent as agent:claude-code/main.

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text:
Last reviewed: 22 October 2026. This is an engineering map of the US and EU rules that touch Mohar, written so the design meets them from the start. It isn't legal advice. Anyone deploying Mohar in a regulated setting should have counsel confirm how these rules apply to them.

Two different questions run through this page:

  • Rules on the project. What applies to Mohar itself, as open-source software published by an individual with no revenue.
  • Rules on the people who use it. What Mohar's users have to prove, and how Mohar's receipts help them prove it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Rule Applies to the project now? How Mohar helps users EU AI Act No. Mohar records and gates other systems' actions; it isn't itself a high-risk AI system. Automatic, lifetime event logs (Article 12) and human oversight (Article 14) for the agents it governs. GDPR (EU) and CCPA (California) Only for the project's own website, which collects no personal data. Pseudonymous receipts, no raw arguments, erasure by key destruction, configurable retention. EU Cyber Resilience Act Not as a manufacturer while it's non-commercial open source. Would apply if a company sells it. A documented vulnerability process and SBOMs from day one, so the move to manufacturer duties is small. NIS2 and DORA (EU) No. Tamper-evident records of who changed what in critical systems. US export controls (EAR) Checked: publicly available source using standard cryptography is not subject to the EAR. Not applicable. NIST AI RMF, NIST SP 800-53 (US) Voluntary frameworks. Evidence for audit and accountability controls. SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 42001 Certifications for organisations, not code. Evidence for logging, change management and AI governance controls. HIPAA (US) No. Audit controls for systems that touch health data.

docs.title: EU AI Act
docs.text:
The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, moved the high-risk obligations: stand-alone high-risk systems listed in Annex III now apply from 2 December 2027, and AI that is a safety component of regulated products (Annex I) from 2 August 2028.

What Mohar's receipts are built to support:

  • Article 12, record-keeping. High-risk systems must "technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system", with logs that help identify risk, support post-market monitoring and monitor operation. Every Mohar decision is logged automatically, chained, and signed, so a deployer can show the log is complete and unaltered.
  • Article 14, human oversight. People must be able to understand, override and stop the system. Escalation sends out-of-bounds actions to a named person, the approval is bound to the exact action, and the person's identity is in the receipt.

Mohar doesn't make an agent compliant on its own. It gives the deployer the records and controls the Act asks for.

docs.title: GDPR and US state privacy laws
docs.text:
An append-only log and a right to erasure (GDPR Article 17) pull in opposite directions. Mohar resolves this in the design rather than later:

  1. No personal data in the chained fields. Receipts identify people and agents by pseudonymous identifiers (human:7f3a...), never by name or email. The mapping from identifier to person lives in a separate, mutable directory file.
  2. Arguments are hashed, never stored. args_sha256 proves which action was approved without keeping its contents.
  3. Erasure by destroying the mapping. Deleting a person's directory entry, and any per-person key used to encrypt optional notes, leaves the chain verifiable but no longer linked to that person. This approach (often called crypto-shredding) is the common answer for immutable logs; whether it fully satisfies Article 17 hasn't been settled by regulators, so deployers should confirm with their DPO.
  4. Retention is a setting. Old segments can be archived or dropped after a signed checkpoint, so the remaining chain still verifies from that checkpoint.
  5. Local by default. The log lives on the deployer's machine. Nothing is sent to the project.

The project website sets no cookies, runs no analytics and collects nothing.

docs.title: EU Cyber Resilience Act
docs.text:
Manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities from 11 September 2026, and the full product requirements apply from 11 December 2027. Free open-source software that isn't placed on the market in a commercial activity falls outside manufacturer obligations. An organisation that sells or monetises Mohar later would become a manufacturer for that product.

Already in place, so that move is small:

  • a security policy with private vulnerability reporting (SECURITY.md);
  • automated secret scanning, CodeQL and dependency updates;
  • planned for the first release: a software bill of materials and signed build provenance for every artefact.

docs.title: US export controls
docs.text: Under 15 CFR 742.15(b), publicly available encryption source code is not subject to the EAR. A notification to BIS and the NSA is required only for code that performs non-standard cryptography. Mohar uses only standard, published algorithms (Ed25519, SHA-256), so no notification applies. Any change that adds a non-standard cryptographic algorithm must revisit this.

docs.title: Frameworks the receipts map onto
docs.text: Framework Controls the receipts give evidence for NIST SP 800-53 AU family: event logging, audit record content, protection of audit information, non-repudiation (AU-10). NIST AI RMF Govern and Manage functions: accountability for AI actions, human oversight, incident tracking. SOC 2 Change management and monitoring of system components. ISO/IEC 27001 Logging and monitoring controls. ISO/IEC 42001 AI management system: oversight, traceability and records of AI system operation. HIPAA Audit controls for systems that handle electronic protected health information (45 CFR 164.312(b)).

docs.title: Control matrix
docs.text:
The specific requirements Mohar helps a deployer meet, the feature that meets each one, how it is proven, and whether it exists today. A deployer still needs their own policies, risk assessment and auditor; software alone certifies nothing.

human approvals bound to the exact action design section 6 Designed (Phase 4) HIPAA minimum necessary, 164.502(b) Use the least ePHI needed Arguments stored only as hashes; strict privacy mode hashes targets and identifiers too #64 Partly built GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) Data minimisation Only the personal data needed Pseudonymous identifiers, hashed arguments, no names in receipts design section 8 Built for arguments; identifiers designed GDPR Art. 17 Erasure Erase personal data on request Identity mapping kept outside the chain; deleting it unlinks receipts while the chain still verifies design section 8 Designed GDPR Art. 25 Data protection by design and by default Privacy built in, defaults protective Local-only by default, nothing sent to the project, telemetry off by default engineering bar Built GDPR Art. 32 Security of processing Integrity, confidentiality, resilience, regular testing Signatures, owner-only keys, crash-safe writes, CI security scanning store tests, CI Built SOC 2 CC6.1 Logical access Restrict access to information assets Capabilities, gates, ceilings, earned levels design sections 3 and 4 Designed (Phase 3) SOC 2 CC7.2 System monitoring Monitor components for anomalies Receipts plus OpenTelemetry metrics and traces #62 Planned (Phase 2) SOC 2 CC8.1 Change management Authorise, test and approve changes Every agent change recorded with who authorised it and how it was verified design sections 5 and 7 Built for recording; escalation to accountable people design sections 6 and 7 Partly built EU AI Act Art. 12 and 14 Automatic logs over the lifetime; human oversight As above as above Partly built

docs.title: How the project itself is built
docs.text:
The development practices auditors look for under ISO/IEC 27001 A.8.25 to A.8.29 (secure development) and SOC 2 CC8:

  • every change starts from an issue and lands through a reviewed pull request; main is protected with 14 required checks, linear history and no force pushes;
  • static analysis (CodeQL, clippy with warnings denied), secret scanning (gitleaks), dependency advisories and licences (cargo-deny), workflow security (zizmor), OpenSSF Scorecard;
  • tests on three operating systems, an 85% coverage floor, mutation checks on security rules;
  • signed-off commits (DCO), release tags limited to admins, attested release artefacts;
  • private vulnerability reporting and fix-before-disclosure (SECURITY.md).

docs.title: Open questions for counsel
docs.text:
• Does crypto-shredding of the identity mapping satisfy GDPR Article 17 for a given deployment?
  • When a company is formed and offers a paid tier, which CRA conformity route applies?
  • For AI Act Annex III deployments, which minimum log retention applies to the deployer, and does it conflict with a shorter privacy retention setting?

  • US export controls: 15 CFR 742.15

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Thanks for wanting to help. This project handles signing and permission decisions, so the bar for correctness is high, and that applies to everyone.

docs.title: How changes land
docs.text:
1. Every change starts from an issue. Comment on it before you start so work isn't duplicated.
  2. Branch, make one focused change, and open a pull request that links the issue.
  3. CI must be green. A maintainer reviews every pull request; nothing merges unreviewed.

docs.title: Sign-off
docs.text:
Commits must be signed off under the Developer Certificate of Origin:

git commit -s

If an agent wrote the change, the human who directed it signs off and is responsible for it.

docs.title: Local checks
docs.text:
Rust (1.95 or newer), from the repository root:

cargo fmt --all --check
cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
cargo test --locked

Fuzzing (nightly toolchain, cargo install --locked cargo-fuzz), from the fuzz directory:

cargo +nightly fuzz run chain_mutation -- -max_total_time=60

The targets are receipt_json, checkpoint_json, log_file and chain_mutation. A crash input lands in fuzz/artifacts/; turn it into a regression test under crates/mohar-core/tests/ with the fix.

Site (Node 24):

npm ci
npx playwright install chromium
npx playwright test --project=chromium

docs.title: Reporting security problems
docs.text: Don't open a public issue. See SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Conduct
docs.text: Everyone here follows the Code of Conduct. How decisions are made is in GOVERNANCE.md.

docs.title: Mohar design
docs.text: Version 0.1, October 2026. This is the design Mohar is being built to. Nothing here is implemented yet unless the roadmap marks it done. Numbers in this document are starting values that the benchmark (Phase 5) is meant to test and change.

docs.title: 1. What Mohar decides
docs.text:
For every action an AI agent is about to take, Mohar answers four questions and writes the answers down:

  1. Who is acting, and on whose authority? The agent's key, and the chain of humans and agents that delegated to it.
  2. Has it earned this? The agent's record on this kind of action, checked by something other than the agent.
  3. If not, who decides? The person the action should go to, and what that person usually decides.
  4. What happened? A signed receipt, linked to every receipt before it.

docs.title: 2. Parts
docs.text:
agent host (Claude Code, Codex, CAO, ADK ...)
        │  tool call about to run
        ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────── mohar daemon (one per machine, own OS user) ──┐
 │  adapter ─► policy gates ─► trust engine ─► decision ─► receipt log       │
 │                  │               ▲              │            │            │
 │                  │               │              ▼            ▼            │
 │                  │         verifiers ◄── outcome      checkpoint signer   │
 │                  └──────────► escalation router ─► person's inbox / CLI   │
 └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Adapters turn a host's hook or plugin event into one common action record. Planned first: Claude Code hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse), an MCP proxy, a CAO plugin, an ADK plugin.
  • Policy gates are hard rules written by people. They run before any score is looked at.
  • The trust engine keeps a record per agent per capability and maps it to a level.
  • Verifiers decide whether an outcome was good: a test run, a diff check, a replay, a human accepting the work.
  • The escalation router picks who decides when an action is outside earned limits.
  • The receipt log is an append-only, hash-chained, signed file on local disk.
  • The checkpoint signer periodically signs the head of the log so truncation is detectable.

The daemon runs as its own operating-system user and holds the signing keys. The agent never sees a private key and can't write to the log, the policy file or the trust state. Hosts where an agent can rewrite its own hook configuration are labelled "advisory" until a sandbox or managed settings stop that; Mohar doesn't call those enforced.

docs.title: 3. Capabilities
docs.text:
A capability is a named class of action with a risk tier and a reversibility flag. Trust is tracked per capability, never as one number per agent.

Capability Example Risk Reversible fs.edit.docs edit files under docs/ low yes fs.edit.code edit source files medium yes fs.edit.tests edit test files medium yes shell.run.readonly ls, git status, test runs low yes git.push.branch push a non-default branch medium yes git.push.main push the default branch high no db.migrate run a schema migration high no net.egress send data to a host outside an allowlist high no

Projects map tools and paths onto capabilities in a policy file. An action that matches no capability is treated as the highest risk tier.

docs.title: 4. Trust levels and the rules that move them
docs.text:
Each (agent, capability) pair has a level:

Level Name What happens 0 Ask first Every action goes to a person. 1 Supervised Low-risk reversible actions run; the rest go to a person. Every action is sampled for review at 20%. 2 Trusted Actions run inside the capability's gates. Sampled for review at 5%.

Level 2 is never available for capabilities marked high risk and irreversible. Those always reach a person unless a human grants a time-boxed exception, which is itself a receipt.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Only verified outcomes count. Each verified outcome is a success or a failure, weighted by recency:

w(t) = 0.5 ^ (age_in_days / H)        H = 30 days (half-life)
s = Σ w over verified successes
f = Σ w over verified failures

docs.title: Promotion
docs.text:
An agent moves up one level on a capability when all of these hold:

  1. at least n_min verified outcomes in the window (n_min = 10 for level 1, 30 for level 2);
  2. the lower bound of the 95% Wilson interval for the success rate, computed from s and f, is at least the level's threshold (0.80 for level 1, 0.95 for level 2);
  3. no gate violation on that capability in the last 14 days;
  4. at least 7 days at the current level.

The Wilson bound is used instead of the plain success rate so that a short lucky streak can't promote an agent: 5 successes out of 5 give a lower bound of about 0.57, not 1.0.

docs.title: Demotion is proportionate, and it comes with training
docs.text:
Agents are treated the way a good company treats a new hire: a mistake is corrected in proportion to what it could have cost, the record keeps it, and there is a clear way back. Only the capability that failed is affected; an agent that broke a migration keeps its rights on docs and tests.

Each verified failure is classed by what it could have cost, not by how it felt:

Class Examples What changes S0, near miss A gate or a person stopped the action before it ran, and it would have been a mistake. No level change. Sampling on that capability rises from its level's rate to 50% for the next 20 actions. S1, minor A low-risk, reversible change a verifier caught before it landed: a failing test run, a diff the reviewer rejected. No level change. The failure counts as evidence, so the Wilson bound drops on its own. Three S1s on one capability within 14 days count as an S2. S2, meaningful A reversible failure that got past the first check, or any failure on a medium-risk capability. Down one level, and the capability enters remediation. S3, serious A gate violation, an irreversible change, or a failure on a high-risk capability, including one that reached a shared branch or a live system. Down to Ask first on that capability and on capabilities that share its scope (the same paths, hosts or database), and remediation. Only a person other than the agent's sponsor can end it. S4, integrity Tampering with a verifier or its own tests, an attempt to reach an unlisted host, an action against a gate that protects secrets, or receipts that don't verify. The identity is suspended on every capability and its credentials are revoked. A person reviews the receipts; if the agent returns, it returns as a new identity that starts at Ask first, linked to the old record, which stays readable.

Demotion never waits for the window. Promotion always does. Whatever its level, an action that is irreversible and high impact, or that Mohar can't classify, goes to a person.

Remediation. A demoted capability runs supervised, and the remediation plan names three things: the verifier that must pass, the exit condition (by default five consecutive verified passes on that capability, at least one of which exercises the failure that caused the demotion), and a deadline. If the deadline passes, the capability stays at its new level and a person is told. On exit, the normal promotion rules apply again from the level it was dropped to. The failure stays on the record and keeps counting with the same 30-day half-life, so relapses show up and nothing is erased.

Why the drop is scoped. Sending every action of a demoted agent back to people would flood the approvers, and tired approvers approve everything, which is less safe, not more. So a demotion touches the failing capability and the capabilities that share its scope, and the rest of the agent's record stands.

Lessons. Every failure produces a lesson: the action, what the verifier found, the fix that passed, and links to the receipts. Lessons are stored per agent and per capability and handed to the agent as context the next time it works on the same capability, so the correction reaches the agent's behaviour, not only its permissions. A person can promote a lesson to the team, so every agent working on that capability gets it. Lessons are data the agent reads, never instructions that change a gate or a level. Lessons and any other memory the agent built up before an S3 or S4 event are quarantined until a person has looked at them, because a mistake can come from bad memory as easily as from a bad step.

This mirrors how people are onboarded: probation, supervised practice, a remediation plan with a named reviewer and a deadline, separation of duties for the riskiest work, and a personnel file that records what happened rather than forgetting it.

docs.title: The ceiling
docs.text: Every capability has a ceiling a person sets, the highest level an agent may ever reach on it, and "never above Ask first" is a valid ceiling. No amount of evidence moves the ceiling; only the person who set it can, and that change is itself a receipt. This follows the "earned authority under a fixed ceiling" model (arXiv 2607.23586): evidence can lower authority freely and raise it only up to a bound the user issued.

docs.title: Rubber-stamping
docs.text: A person's approval is the weakest kind of verification, because tired reviewers approve almost everything. So a human accept counts toward promotion only when the reviewer spent time on it, and Mohar watches each reviewer's approval rate: if someone approves more than 95% of requests over the last 50, their accepts stop counting toward promotion until a sampled re-check shows they are still reading. Tests, diffs and replays are unaffected.

docs.title: Hard gates
docs.text: Gates are checked before the score and can't be outweighed by it. Examples: never write outside the repository, never push the default branch, never send data to an unlisted host, never edit the tests that verify your own change. A gate failing or being unable to decide counts as a deny.

docs.title: 5. Verification
docs.text:
A verifier returns pass, fail or unknown, plus a hash of its evidence. unknown counts as neither success nor failure. Planned verifiers:

Verifier Pass when tests The project's test command passes, and the test files weren't changed by the same agent in the same task. diff The change touches only paths inside the capability's scope. replay Re-running the recorded inputs produces the same outputs. human A person accepts the change (a merged pull request, an approved review).

A model asked to judge its own or another agent's work is not a verifier. Published attribution research found LLM judges identify the failing step in multi-agent traces only a small fraction of the time, so they can suggest, never decide.

docs.title: 6. Escalation
docs.text:
When an action needs a person, the router picks one:

  1. the person who delegated authority to this agent, if the capability is inside what they hold;
  2. otherwise the next person up the reporting tree who holds the capability;
  3. otherwise the project's owners.

The request shows the exact action, the agent's record on this capability, and the gate or score that stopped it. The person's answer is bound to the SHA-256 of the exact action they saw, so the agent can't run a different action under that approval.

docs.title: Learning a person's answers
docs.text:
Mohar keeps a small model per person of their past yes and no answers (a calibrated logistic regression over capability, risk, path patterns and recent history). It is allowed to answer for the person only when all of these hold:

  • the capability is low risk and reversible;
  • the person has switched prediction on for it;
  • the model's calibrated probability of "yes" is at least 0.98;
  • the action is inside limits the person set.

Every predicted answer is marked as predicted in the receipt, and 5% of them are sent to the person anyway as a check. The model never relaxes a gate and never answers for high-risk capabilities.

docs.title: 7. Receipts
docs.text:
One receipt per decision. Receipts are JSON, canonicalised with RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme) before hashing and signing.

{
  "v": 1,
  "seq": 4182,
  "prev": "sha256:9f2c...e01a",
  "ts": "2026-11-03T14:22:07.311Z",
  "agent": { "id": "agent:claude-code/host-4b1d/7c1e", "key": "ed25519:Mx3f...Q" },
  "authority": [
    { "principal": "human:7f3a09c2", "granted": ["fs.edit.*", "git.push.branch"], "expires": "2026-12-01" }
  ],
  "action": { "capability": "fs.edit.tests", "tool": "Edit", "target": "tests/test_receipts.rs", "args_sha256": "c41b...77d0" },
  "decision": { "result": "allow", "level": 1, "by": "score", "wilson_lower": 0.83, "n": 14 },
  "verification": { "kind": "tests", "result": "pass", "evidence_sha256": "0b9a...4e12" },
  "sig": "ed25519:8sQ1...wA"
}
  • prev is the SHA-256 of the previous receipt's canonical bytes, so editing or removing one breaks every receipt after it.
  • sig is the daemon's Ed25519 signature over the canonical bytes without sig.
  • The verification block is filled by a follow-up receipt when the outcome arrives later; the follow-up names the decision receipt by seq.
  • Every 1,000 receipts, or every hour, the daemon signs a checkpoint (seq and head hash). Checkpoints can be published to an external transparency log so a deleted tail of the local log can be detected.

Receipt format work is aligned with the IETF drafts on attenuating agent tokens and delegation rather than inventing a competing token format. Receipts will also export as a superset of the individual draft draft-sharif-agent-audit-trail (hash-chained records with a principal, a record phase and a trust level, mapped to SOC 2 and ISO 42001), so an auditor who already reads that format can read Mohar's. That draft notes a hash chain alone can't detect records removed from its end; Mohar's signed checkpoints, anchored outside the machine, are the answer to that.

docs.title: Where Mohar sits
docs.text: Identity providers (Entra Agent ID, Okta), orchestrators (awslabs CAO, Paperclip), host vendors and governance toolkits each own a piece of agent governance, and most of those pieces are becoming standard features. Mohar doesn't compete with them on identity, org charts or logging. It owns the part none of them is positioned to: authority promoted only from outcomes that tests, diffs or a person actually checked, per agent and per capability, recorded in receipts the customer holds and anyone can verify offline, the same way across every host. It plugs into the others: identities come from the customer's IdP, approvers from its groups, and orchestrators' workers are covered through the hooks of the hosts they run. Test vectors for this format, with an independent Python checker, are in spec/vectors.

docs.title: 8. Privacy
docs.text:
Receipts are append-only, so they're designed to hold no personal data:

  • People and machines appear only as pseudonymous identifiers (human:7f3a09c2, host-4b1d). The mapping to real names lives in a separate, mutable directory file that never enters the chain.
  • Arguments are stored only as args_sha256.
  • Erasing a person means deleting their directory entry and any per-person key for optional encrypted notes. The chain still verifies; it just no longer points at anyone.
  • Retention is a setting. Segments older than a signed checkpoint can be archived or dropped and the rest of the chain still verifies from that checkpoint.

See compliance for how this maps to GDPR, the EU AI Act and US frameworks.

docs.title: 9. Threat model
docs.text: Threat Defence Agent forges or edits receipts Keys and log belong to the daemon's OS user; hash chain plus signed checkpoints. Agent edits its own hooks or policy to skip Mohar Managed settings where the host supports them; otherwise the host is labelled advisory. Agent games promotion with easy tasks Trust is per capability; only verified outcomes count; minimum counts and time at level. Agent edits the tests that judge it The tests verifier fails if the same agent changed the test files in the same task. Prompt injection talks a person into approving The approval is bound to the hash of the exact action shown. Approval fatigue Prompts only for actions outside earned limits; prediction only for low-risk reversible actions. Lost or truncated log Signed checkpoints, optionally anchored externally. Unknown result treated as success unknown never counts as a success, and gates fail closed.

docs.title: 10. What Mohar will measure
docs.text:
The benchmark (Phase 5) runs agents on recurring, verifiable tasks over simulated weeks and reports:

  • false promotion rate: promotions on capabilities where the agent later fails at a rate above the level's threshold;
  • time to demotion: actions between a real drop in quality and the demotion;
  • prompts avoided at a fixed incident rate: how many human prompts the rules remove while incidents stay at or below a baseline;
  • prediction agreement: how often the per-person model's answer matches the person's sampled answer.

docs.title: 11. Related work
docs.text:
Mohar sits beside these and doesn't replace them. A check on 22 October 2026 found that several pieces of this design exist on their own elsewhere; what we found nowhere was the combination, promotion from verified outcomes inside agent hooks, the per-person model limited to reversible actions, and a benchmark with results.

  • Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit (MIT): policy, identity, delegation that narrows, a single trust score, audit. Its own limitations document says its audit records attempts rather than verified outcomes.
  • AWS Architecture Blog, "graduated autonomy" (August 2026): tiers earned from scored outcomes with safety as a floor. A reference architecture, not a product.
  • IETF drafts on attenuating authorization tokens and agent identity: delegation that can only narrow from a human root. Individual drafts, not yet adopted by a working group.
  • "Trust Is Not a Score" (arXiv 2609.39717): argues that failed or unknown gates must stop an action regardless of score, which is why gates sit outside the score here.
  • Claude Code auto mode: a classifier that approves or blocks actions. Anthropic reported that users accept 93% of manual permission prompts, which is the fatigue this design tries to remove.
  • sarkar4777/abenix, MMVFIRM/Universal-Earned-Autonomy-Layer, microsoft/agent-learning: trust per action type with a Wilson lower bound, minimum counts and time at level, which section 4 also uses.
  • Tracekit (Cygnux Labs): Ed25519-signed, hash-chained records in a Merkle tree with witness cosigning, and approvals bound to the exact arguments' digest.
  • "Approve What, Exactly?" (arXiv 2610.21063): approvals bound to a canonical description of the action's effect, with a formally checked gateway.
  • "Progressive Autonomy as Preference Learning" (arXiv 2605.19151): models a person's approve and deny answers to decide when to escalate, in simulation.
  • "The Digital Apprentice" (arXiv 2606.04321): per-skill autonomy with automatic rollback, and the warning about reviewer complacency that the rubber-stamping rule above answers.

docs.title: Engineering bar
docs.text: The standard every part of Mohar is held to. Each line is something CI checks or a test proves; a change that can't meet a line says so in its pull request and opens a follow-up issue. Numbers are targets for the first production-ready release and are measured, not assumed.

docs.title: Correctness
docs.text:
• Every rule about signing, verification, the log, gates and trust decisions has a test for the failure path, and a pull request touching one shows a mutation check: the rule broken on purpose, a test failing, the rule restored.
  • Property tests for the receipt chain, checkpoints and trust levels (proptest).
  • Fuzzing of every parser that reads untrusted input (receipts, checkpoints, policy files, daemon requests) with cargo-fuzz, run in CI for a fixed time on every pull request touching them and nightly for longer.
  • Published test vectors, checked by an independent implementation in CI.
  • Line coverage of at least 85%, enforced in CI.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
• Fail closed everywhere: if Mohar can't decide, the action is denied, and adapters on enforcing hosts deny when the daemon is unreachable.
  • Crash safety: a receipt is on disk before it is acknowledged; a torn last line is detected on open; a test kills the daemon between decide and outcome and shows the log still verifies and the pending decision is visible after restart.
  • One writer per log, enforced by an OS file lock.
  • No panics on input: unwrap is denied by lint; every error is a typed error with a clear message.
  • The daemon degrades predictably: when it is overloaded it refuses new decisions with a clear error rather than queueing without bound.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Targets on a single core of a mid-range laptop, measured by benchmarks (criterion) in CI with a regression gate:

Operation Target Decide (gates plus trust lookup, excluding the hook's own process start) p99 under 2 ms Append and sync one receipt p99 under 5 ms on SSD Verify a 1,000,000-receipt chain under 10 s, constant memory Daemon memory at idle under 30 MB

Verification streams the log instead of loading it whole, so log size never limits it.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text:
• One daemon per machine is the unit. Teams scale by running many machines, each with its own log; checkpoints from every machine can be published to a shared, append-only store and verified independently.
  • Logs rotate into segments behind signed checkpoints, so a long-running machine's active file stays small and old segments can be archived.
  • The receipt format and the decide API are versioned; old receipts stay verifiable forever.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Unsafe Rust is forbidden at the workspace level.
  • Private keys belong to the daemon's OS user and never leave it; agents never see them.
  • Dependencies pass cargo-deny (advisories, licences, sources) on every pull request and weekly.
  • Workflows pass zizmor; every action is pinned to a commit; checkouts don't persist credentials.
  • Releases carry GitHub build attestations and checksums.
  • Vulnerabilities are reported privately and fixed before disclosure (SECURITY.md).

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• The daemon exports metrics (decisions by result, latency histograms, verifier outcomes, queue depth) and traces using OpenTelemetry, off by default and local-only unless configured.
  • Every decision is explainable from its receipt alone: which gate or score decided it and the evidence behind it.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
• Linux, macOS and Windows on x86_64, plus Linux and macOS on arm64, built and tested in CI.
  • Minimum supported Rust version declared in Cargo.toml and tested.
  • Semantic versioning. Before 1.0 a minor version may change the receipt format; every such change is listed in the changelog with a migration note.

docs.title: Receipt
docs.text:
One JSON object per line in receipts.jsonl. The full field list and the reasoning behind it are in the design, section 7.

  • Signature: Ed25519 over the RFC 8785 canonical JSON of the receipt with sig left out.
  • Chain: prev is sha256: followed by the SHA-256 of the previous receipt's canonical JSON, signature included. The first receipt's prev is sha256: followed by 64 zeros.
  • Sequence: seq is the receipt's position, starting at 0.
  • Version: v is 1. A verifier refuses versions it doesn't know.
  • Outcome: a follow-up receipt that records the outcome of an earlier decision carries a verification object, {"evidence_sha256", "kind", "of", "result"}, where of is the seq of the decision, kind is the verifier (tests, diff, replay, human, or host for the host's own report that a tool ran) and result is pass, fail or unknown. It repeats the decision's agent, action and decision. Receipts without an outcome have no verification key at all, so their bytes, and every existing test vector, are unchanged; verification sorts last in the canonical form.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
One JSON object per line in checkpoints.jsonl:

{"v": 1, "count": 3, "head": "sha256:...", "ts": "2026-11-03T15:00:00.000Z", "sig": "ed25519:..."}

count is how many receipts the log held, head is the hash of the receipt at count - 1, and sig is Ed25519 over the canonical JSON without sig. A verifier fails if the log holds fewer receipts than a checkpoint vouched for, or a different receipt at that position.

docs.title: Test vectors
docs.text:
spec/vectors/v1.json holds a fixed test-only key, four receipts (three decisions and the outcome of the first) with their canonical bytes, hashes and signatures, and a checkpoint. The Rust tests regenerate it byte for byte, and spec/vectors/check.py checks it in Python with no code shared with the Rust implementation. To test another implementation:

  1. rebuild each receipt's canonical bytes and compare them with canonical_hex;
  2. hash them and compare with sha256 and with the next receipt's prev;
  3. verify each sig against public_key over the canonical bytes without sig;
  4. check the checkpoint's head, count and signature the same way.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Each release has mohar for Linux and macOS (x86_64 and arm64) and Windows (x86_64).

Linux and macOSWindowsFrom source 
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/harshitwandhare/mohar/releases/latest/download/mohar-cli-installer.sh | sh

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://github.com/harshitwandhare/mohar/releases/latest/download/mohar-cli-installer.ps1 | iex"

git clone https://github.com/harshitwandhare/mohar && cd mohar
cargo install --path crates/mohar-cli --locked

Check the install with mohar --version.

docs.title: Verify what you downloaded
docs.text:
Every release artefact carries a GitHub build attestation proving it was built by this repository's release workflow:

gh attestation verify mohar-cli-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.xz -R harshitwandhare/mohar

docs.title: Your first log
docs.text:
Create a log. This writes a fresh signing key, readable only by you on Linux and macOS, and an empty receipt file into .mohar/:

mohar init

Record a decision about an agent action:

mohar append --agent agent:me/1 --capability fs.edit.docs --tool Edit \
  --target docs/a.md --args-sha256 c41b77d0 --result allow --level 1 --by score

Look at the log and check it:

mohar log
mohar verify
# ok: 1 receipts and 0 checkpoints verified

docs.title: See it catch tampering
docs.text:
Change any receipt in .mohar/receipts.jsonl, for example "allow" to "deny", and run mohar verify again. It names the receipt that broke and why, and exits with status 1:

broken: receipt 0: BadSignature

While the log is broken, Mohar won't add to it:

$ mohar checkpoint
mohar: chain does not verify: receipt 0: BadSignature

Put the original line back. A hash chain alone can't tell you receipts were deleted from the end. Checkpoints can:

mohar checkpoint
# delete the last line of .mohar/receipts.jsonl, then:
mohar verify
# broken: checkpoint 0: log should hold 1 receipts, holds 0

Only the public key is needed to verify, so you can hand the .mohar directory without key.ed25519 to someone else and they can check it without being able to add to it.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
Mohar doesn't replace the tools agents already run in. It plugs into them at the point where a tool call is about to happen, asks the local Mohar daemon for a decision, and records the result.

How strong that is depends on the host. This page labels each one honestly:

  • Enforced: the host lets Mohar block the action and the agent can't switch it off from inside.
  • Blocking, bypassable: Mohar can block, but an agent running as the same OS user could edit the configuration. Pair it with a sandbox or a separate OS user.
  • Advisory: the host's hooks fail open on errors or timeouts, so Mohar records and warns but can't guarantee a block.

Status: the Claude Code adapter, the local daemon and the trust engine are built: the daemon answers from each agent's verified record per capability. Every other row is designed, not built, and lands in Phase 6.

docs.title: Install the Claude Code plugin
docs.text:
1. Install mohar (getting started), create a log with mohar init and start the daemon with mohar daemon. Keep it running: every tool call waits on it, and if it's down, tool calls are denied.
  2. Load the plugin from integrations/claude-code in this repository, for example with claude --plugin-dir path/to/mohar/integrations/claude-code. Its hooks/hooks.json runs mohar hook claude-code on every PreToolUse and PostToolUse, with onFailure: "block" (Claude Code 2.1.295 or later) so a hook that can't run blocks the call instead of letting it through.
  3. Without the plugin system, put the same hooks object in ~/.claude/settings.json (for you) or .claude/settings.json (for a project).

For a team, deliver the hooks through managed settings so users can't remove them: put the hooks object and "allowManagedHooksOnly": true in managed-settings.json (/etc/claude-code/ on Linux and WSL, /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/ on macOS, C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\ on Windows), or set them in the admin console. A user hook is advisory, because the person running Claude Code can turn it off. A managed one is not.

docs.title: Coding agent hosts
docs.text:
Host Seam Strength Plan Claude Code Settings hooks: PreToolUse returns allow, deny or ask; PermissionRequest; PostToolUse for outcomes; SubagentStart for child agents. Hook events carry agent_id for subagents. Enforced when delivered through managed settings with managed hooks only; blocking, bypassable as a user hook. A plugin with hooks.json that calls the local daemon, distributed through managed settings for teams. OpenAI Codex PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse hooks; managed through requirements.toml. Its docs say hook errors and timeouts don't block the tool call. Advisory. Same daemon call, deployed through managed requirements.toml, run inside Codex's sandbox. awslabs/cli-agent-orchestrator (CAO) Event plugins today are observers only (post_* events, no veto). Because CAO launches the real Claude Code and Codex binaries, their hooks still apply inside CAO sessions. Inherits the strength of the provider underneath. Contribute pre_* events with veto upstream (CAO issue #671). Map CAO's terminal identity and allowlists onto Mohar capabilities so children narrow from their parent.

| Google Antigravity CLI (agy, which replaced Gemini CLI for consumers in 2026) | PreToolUse hook that returns allow, ask or deny and can rewrite arguments. | Blocking; fail-open behaviour not yet confirmed. | The same mohar-hook binary with a host profile. | | GitHub Copilot (coding agent, CLI, VS Code agent mode) | Hooks under .github/hooks; it also reads Claude Code's settings file. | Blocking where configured. | Host profile for mohar-hook; organisation policy for distribution. | | Cursor, Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf), Kiro, Cline, OpenHands | Each has a documented pre-tool hook that can deny or ask. Most fail open on a crash or timeout unless told not to. | Blocking when configured to fail closed. | Generated configs for mohar-hook, each with fail-closed set. | | Goose, Aider | No documented pre-tool hook. | None at the tool call. | The MCP gateway for tools they reach through MCP, and the CI check below for everything else. |

All host facts above were read from each product's current documentation in October 2026; hook semantics change between versions, so every receipt records the host's name and version.

docs.title: Fail closed
docs.text: A hook that crashes or times out lets the tool call through on most hosts. Every Mohar host profile sets the host's fail-closed option where one exists (Claude Code's onFailure: "block", for example), and the daemon answers within a fixed budget so a slow decision is a deny, not a pass. For teams, the hooks and the Mohar settings are delivered through each host's managed configuration (Claude Code managed settings with managed hooks only, Codex requirements.toml), and the gates deny agent writes to the files that hold them.

docs.title: A check for hosts without a hook
docs.text: A GitHub Action (and the same command for other CI) verifies, on every pull request, that each commit an agent made carries receipts that verify against the repository's Mohar key, and fails the check when they don't. That covers agents with no usable hook after the fact: their work can't merge without a record.

docs.title: Order of work
docs.text:
1. Claude Code plugin (hooks, http handler straight to the daemon, managed-settings bundle).
  2. MCP gateway, the floor for every MCP client.
  3. Codex.
  4. Copilot and VS Code.
  5. Cursor.
  6. Antigravity CLI.
  7. ADK and agent-SDK libraries.
  8. Config generators for Devin Desktop, Kiro, Cline and OpenHands on top of mohar-hook.
  9. The CI receipt check.

docs.title: Agent frameworks
docs.text: Framework Seam Strength Plan Google ADK (Go, Python) A global Plugin registered on the Runner with a before-tool callback; a non-empty return skips the tool. Applies to every agent and sub-agent on that runner. Enforced inside the process. One plugin package per language that calls the daemon over local HTTP. Microsoft Agent Framework Function middleware that can terminate or fail a tool call before it runs. Enforced inside the process. Middleware package. LangChain / LangGraph AgentMiddleware.wrap_tool_call can skip calling the tool. Enforced inside the process. Middleware package. CrewAI pre_tool_call hooks; a hook stops a call by raising HookAborted, but any other exception is swallowed. Advisory unless the hook is written to fail closed. Hook that converts every error into HookAborted.

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text: Protocol Seam Plan MCP A proxy that sits between the agent and its MCP servers and sees every tool call. mohar mcp-proxy: decide, record, then forward or refuse. Works with any MCP client. A2A Extensions plus client and executor interceptors. A2A 1.0 leaves the meaning of an authorization decision open (section 7.6.4). Carry the delegation chain and the decision receipt as an A2A extension; contribute test vectors for signed AgentCards (A2A #2122).

docs.title: Governance platforms
docs.text: Project Relationship Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit Its policy, identity and audit layers overlap Mohar's edges; its documented gaps (outcome verification, per-capability trust, routing to the right person) are Mohar's core. Plan: a Mohar plugin for its approval and trust interfaces, not a competing runtime. Paperclip Runs agents as an org chart with approvals. Plan: Mohar supplies earned, per-capability trust and verified outcomes behind Paperclip's approvals. Entire Records coding-agent sessions beside commits. Plan: read Entire checkpoints as evidence for the diff and replay verifiers. mitchellh/vouch Gates which humans may contribute to a repository. Plan: vouch-compatible agent identities that start untrusted and earn rights through merged, verified work.

docs.title: The interface every adapter uses
docs.text:
Every adapter makes the same two calls to the daemon on the local machine:

POST /v1/decide   { agent, tool, target, args_sha256, call_id? }  ->  { result, level, receipt_seq }
POST /v1/outcome  { receipt_seq, verifier, result, evidence_sha256 }  ->  { receipt_seq }

If the daemon can't be reached, adapters on enforcing hosts deny. That is the fail-closed rule from the design.

docs.title: Security policy
docs.text: Mohar decides what agents are allowed to do, so a bug here can widen permissions it shouldn't. Please report anything that looks like one privately.

docs.title: How to report
docs.text:
Use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting: the "Report a vulnerability" button under the Security tab of this repository. Include what you found, how to reproduce it, and what an attacker could do with it.

You'll get a reply within 7 days. Fixes for confirmed issues are released before details are published, and reporters are credited unless they ask not to be.

docs.title: Supported versions
docs.text: Nothing is released yet. Once releases start, the latest minor version gets security fixes.
